# Methods {#sec-methods}

This chapter describes the experimental design of the thesis. Every tabular foundation model in the experiments is evaluated frozen. The pretrained weights are used exactly as published, and no fine-tuning or any other gradient update is applied [@thomas2024localpfn_retrieval_finetuning]. The only element that varies is test-time context construction, meaning which labelled training rows fill the context window and at what class ratio. As @sec-bg-pfn established, the context is the only task-specific information the model conditions on, so the context is the natural point of intervention.

The research questions of @sec-intro-rqs decompose into pairwise contrasts between the four context-construction conditions C1 to C4 which are further elaborated in @sec-methods-conditions. This decomposition is the spine of the research design. The rest of the chapter defines the conditions and the machinery that runs them.

## Experimental conditions {#sec-methods-conditions}

Condition 1 (random) fills the context with a uniform random subsample of the training set, drawn up to the model's context limit. The fraud ratio of the context thus follows the natural prevalence of the data. This is the standard practice whose cost @sec-context-waste quantified, and it serves as the baseline for every other condition.

Condition 2 (stratified) balances the context toward a 50/50 class split. All available fraud rows enter the context, capped at half of the window, and the remaining slots are filled with randomly drawn legitimate rows. On datasets whose training split holds fewer fraud rows than half the window, the realised ratio therefore stays below 50/50. <!-- TODO: adding a inline r that fetches the real fraud ratios. And list them then here. --> Both classes are still drawn at random, so the contrast between C2 and C1 gives the effect of rebalancing the classes while relevance is held fixed.

Condition 3 (kNN control) fills the context by kNN retrieval around clusters of the scored test transactions, without touching the class ratio (@sec-methods-rap). The realised fraud share is therefore not fixed but fluctuates with the local neighbourhood of each cluster. <!-- TODO: adding a inline r that fetches the real fraud ratios from different runs. And list them then here. --> The contrast between C3 and C1 consequently varies relevance without holding the ratio fixed. Relevance is isolated cleanly only by the ratio-matched ablation described in @sec-app-relevance-ablation. The unmatched form is kept deliberately, because it asks a question of its own. Does a TFM need to see fraudulent transactions from far regions of the feature space, or is the relevant region alone enough?

Condition C4 is the full RAP configuration. Retrieval becomes stratified, with a separate kNN retriever per class, so that relevant observations are drawn from both classes. On top of this, the fraud ratio of the context is enforced and swept over 5 %, 10 %, 20 %, 30 % and 50 %. When the unique fraud rows near a cluster run out before the quota is filled, fraud rows are duplicated by sampling with replacement. This oversampling is part of the method rather than a fallback. The duplication this policy introduces is quantified independently of retrieval by the sweep of @sec-app-c2-sweep, and the ablation of @sec-app-relevance-ablation adds a natural-ratio retrieval arm so the selection mechanism is also tested without ratio enforcement. The step from C3 to C4 is thus not just a single-factor change, it both enforces the ratio and swaps mixed retrieval for stratified retrieval. The sweep within C4 in turn isolates ratio tuning on a fixed retrieval mechanism.

The GBDT baselines run under C1 only and are trained on the full training set. The context limit is an inherent property of TFMs, so the most informative comparison for RQ1 is the full-data GBDT against the context-limited TFM. The context budget is 10,000 rows for TabPFN v2, the hard limit of its checkpoint. The remaining models run at a budget of roughly 50,000 rows. This figure is a design choice made for cross-model comparability, not the maximum of every checkpoint. <!-- TODO: future abblation to test all models at their best condition with the biggest context windows possible -->

## The Retrieval Augmented Prediction pipeline {#sec-methods-rap}

@fig-rap-overview gives an overview of the pipeline. Retrieval operates per group of test transactions rather than per test batch. The scored test set is clustered with k-means, and the number of groups $G$ is chosen by the silhouette score over $k = 2$ to $20$, computed on a seeded subsample of roughly 5,000 test rows. The chosen $G$ and its silhouette score are recorded with every run as `n_groups` and `group_silhouette`.

The motivation for this granularity is context reuse, not the number of model fits. The expensive operation in TFM inference is encoding the roughly 50,000-row context, a cost paid inside every prediction pass whenever the encoded context is not cached. Building one context per group caps the number of distinct contexts at $G$, which makes caching of the encoded context (the transformer's key-value cache) possible and would translate into significant prediction speedups in a production setting. A finer granularity, such as one context per test batch, would trade away exactly this reusability for tighter locality; per-batch retrieval is left for future research.

The retriever itself, shown in @fig-rap-overview, is a brute-force nearest-neighbour search over the training features, standardised with a scaler fit on the training split only. Cosine distance is the default metric, and the retrieval depth is derived from the context size, usually 50,000 rows. Under C3 the retrieval is mixed: the nearest training rows enter the context regardless of class, with a guard that injects the globally nearest fraud or legitimate row when a group's context would otherwise contain a single class. Under C4 the retrieval is class-conditional, with a separate retriever per class, and the fraud quota is filled by sampling with replacement when the pool of unique fraud rows near a group runs out, the oversampling policy already defined in @sec-methods-conditions. Both retrieval conditions run only on TabPFN v3 and TabICLv2, the two best-performing models under C1 and C2.

## Models {#sec-methods-models}

The experiments evaluate five TFMs: TabPFN v2, TabPFN 2.5, TabPFN 2.6, TabPFN v3 and TabICLv2 [@hollmann2025accurate_tabular_foundation_model; @grinsztajn2025tabpfn25_arxiv; @priorlabs2026tabpfn26_model_card; @grinsztajn2026tabpfn3_technical_report; @qu2026tabiclv2]. TabPFN v2 runs at a context budget of 10,000 rows and TabICLv2 at roughly 48,000 rows; TabPFN 2.5, 2.6 and v3 run at a budget of roughly 50,000 rows. As stated in @sec-methods-conditions, the 50,000-row figure is more of a design choice for cross-model comparability than a hard limit of every checkpoint. The installed TabPFN v3 checkpoint accepts up to 1,000,000 context rows and TabPFN 2.6 up to 100,000, both verified from the inference configuration of the `tabpfn` library version 8.0.8 used throughout, while TabPFN v2 (10,000) and TabPFN 2.5 (50,000) run at their checkpoints' own caps. TabICLv2 has no checkpoint cap at all; its authors validate inference on million-scale tables [@qu2026tabiclv2], so its 48,000-row figure is likewise our design budget rather than a model limit. All models run on a single GPU (NVIDIA RTX 5070), and the library version is recorded with every run, so no reported result silently mixes library versions.

The GBDT baselines are XGBoost and CatBoost [@chen2016xgboost_scalable_tree_boosting; @dorogush2018catboost]. Both are class-weighted, with the positive-class weight (`scale_pos_weight`) set from the training labels, and run with fixed strong defaults rather than library defaults: 2,000 trees, depth 6, learning rate 0.05, row and column subsampling of 0.8, and early stopping on PR-AUC with a patience of 50 rounds on a 10 % stratified validation split. Neither the GBDTs nor the TFMs are tuned per dataset, so the comparison is a zero-shot TFM against a fixed-default GBDT. Comparisons against per-dataset tuned models are taken from the literature instead rather than duplicated. A direct comparison between the tuned models and TFMs is in @#sec-results-sota.

## Splitting protocol {#sec-methods-splits}

Each dataset is split into training and test sets with a seeded stratified 80/20 split. Banksim is instead split by its customer column, with every customer assigned wholly to one side of the split, because the encoded customer identifier would otherwise act as an entity key that leaks labels from training to test [@lopezrojas2014banksim]. <!-- TODO: double check that no other dataset has customer columns --> Fifar uses its fixed published split. The amounts of negatives on every dataset has been capped to 30,000. This means that the eu_cc test_sets were scored fully. The speedup gained from this sumpsampling was substantial in paysim it offered approximately 42 <!-- inl R code that calculates the speedup form results --> times speed ups comapred to a full test-set scoring. <!-- TODO: Idea for appendix ablation or future research. Does the amount of negative samples affect the scoring of positive test set values. Do a sweep form just positive to 1000-to-1 positive underrepresentations. -->

The time columns are deliberately kept as features. Under a random split this is a temporal-leakage threat: the temporal regularities shown in @fig-fraud-rate-time are available to every model and may inflate the ranking metrics of the separable datasets, paysim and eu_cc in particular. The threat is treated as a limitation in the discussion and bounded by a separate temporal-generalisation ablation found in @sec-app-second. In this ablations baf is split by its time following the dataset's published protocol [@jesus2022baf_arxiv].

## Evaluation metrics

The primary evalution metrics for the models are prevalence corrected PR-AUC, and recall at 1% an 5%. The prevalence has to be corrected in measurements due to the negative class sumsampling explained in @sec-methods-splits. This chapter explains the how the evaluation metrics are constructed.

Let $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$ be the scored test sample with labels $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$, $P = \sum_i y_i$ positives and $N = n - P$ negatives,and let $s_i = f(x_i)$ be the model's fraud score for row $i$. A threshold $t$ classifies row $i$ as fraud iff $s_i \ge t$. The threshold-dependent counts are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{TP}(t) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}[s_i \ge t]y_i \\
\mathrm{FP}(t) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}[s_i \ge t](1 - y_i)
\end{aligned}
$$

Then the thredhold dependent rates can be trivially derived from these:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{TPR}(t) &= \frac{TP}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}[s_i \ge t]}\\
\mathrm{FPR}(t) &= \frac{FP}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}[s_i \ge t]}
\end{aligned}
$$
Then we are to derive the prevalence calibrated precision following @siblini2020_metrics example. W let $\pi$ denote the fraud prevalence of the full test split. Precision at threshold $t$, calibrated to prevalence $\pi$, follows from Bayes':

$$
\mathrm{Prec}_{\pi}(t) = \frac
{\pi~\mathrm{TPR}(t)}
{\pi~\mathrm{TPR}(t) + (1 - \pi)~\mathrm{FPR}(t)}
$${#eq-prec}

Then the Recall doesn't need to get calibration as it is no dependent on the negative ($y_i = 0$) class.

$$
\mathrm{Rec}(t)=\frac{TP(t)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_i }
$${#eq-rec}

Only the distinct observed score values yield distinct operating points, so the threshold set is $\{t_1 > t_2 > \dots > t_K\} = \{s_i\}$ with tied scores collapsed into a single threshold and by definition $Rec(t_K) = 1$.

The precision-recall curve is the set of points $\bigl(Rec(t_k), \mathrm{Prec}_{\pi}(t_k)\bigr)$ with the points defined from @eq-rec and @eq-prec. The area under this curve (AUC-PR) is, in idealised form, the integral of precision over recall. [@davis2006relationship_pr_roc]

$$
\mathrm{AUC\text{-}PR}_{\pi} = \int_{0}^{1} \mathrm{Prec}_{\pi}(r) \, \mathrm{d}r
$$
which we estimate by average precision, the right-continuous step-sum over the empirical operating points ( assuming $\mathrm{Rec}(0) = 0$):

$$
\mathrm{AP}_{\pi} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \bigl( \mathrm{Rec}(t_k)-\mathrm{Rec}(t_{k-1}) \bigr) \mathrm{Prec}_{\pi}(t_k)
$${#eq-ap}

$\mathrm{AP}$ weights each precision value by the recall gained at that threshold linear interpolation between PR points is deliberately not used, as the estimate is optimistically biased [@davis2006relationship_pr_roc].

## The experimental grid {#sec-methods-grid}

The full design consists of running the datasets of @sec-data-datasets with different seeds, models and conditions. This means that the datasets (excluding fifar, which is run with one seed) are run with multiple random seeds. The state of the art models are run with ten different seeds under C1 and C2 and the rest are run with three seeds; C3 and C4 run on the three seeds shared by all models. The C1 and C2 run on all five TFMs, while C3 and C4 run only on TabPFN v3 and TabICLv2, as stated in @sec-methods-rap. Together with the GBDT baselines this core grid holds 460 <!-- TODO: use a count script and count straight from the source packages. --> runs. On fifar the split stays fixed across these seeds, so the seed variation there reflects only the random context draws.

Two protocol conventions recur in the results chapter. First, the RAP design-space sweep replaces the automatic silhouette grouping of @sec-methods-rap with a forced group count $G$ over $\{8, 16, 32, 64\}$, crossed with the distance metric (cosine or euclidean), the C4 fraud-ratio sweep and both retrieval-capable models, on the three datasets where the conditions separate (eu_cc, banksim and paysim) with three seeds each. This yields 720 runs over 240 configurations. Second, where a results table summarises all conditions at once, it uses a fixed pivot protocol: values are restricted to the seeds C4 ran, each cell takes the better of TabPFN v3 and TabICLv2 averaged over those seeds, and C4 is shown at its best swept ratio. This selection favours the retrieval conditions, so the pivot overstates rather than understates them.

The statistical treatment of the grid is descriptive. Per-dataset values are reported as the mean over seeds with its standard deviation, with fifar contributing a single split. Paired comparisons, such as the C2 minus C1 difference in PR-AUC over the 65 paired core runs, are reported with a confidence interval rather than a bare mean, but the deltas are read as descriptive summaries rather than formal tests, since runs of different models share the same dataset-seed splits and are therefore not independent observations. Win, tie and loss are here defined as an absolute difference below 0.005 counting as a tie. Any effect smaller than one seed standard deviation is flagged as directional rather than significant at three seeds.
